sources.citation: Fatihi, A. R. 1987. Economy of articulation in Mewati phonology. PhD thesis, Aligarh Muslim University, Dept. of Linguistics (supervisor Abdul Azim). 371 pp. Shodhganga handle 10603/52319.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Columbia-school 'Phonology as Human Behavior' study of articulator economy (voicing, aspiration, nasality, apertures), with data deliberately restricted to monosyllabic words (Introduction pp. 35-37). No hit for stress/accent/suprasegmental/prosody in the text of any chapter; the existing scanned layer is badly garbled, so this silence is weak evidence, but the design (monosyllables only, no prosody chapter in the TOC) makes a stress statement unlikely.

sources.citation: Bharadwaj, D. R. 1974. Descriptive analysis of Mewati. PhD thesis, Deccan College Post-Graduate and Research Institute / University of Poona (supervisor Nilmadhav Sen). 356 pp. Shodhganga handle 10603/149220.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Chapter I Phonology (pp. 1-77) opens: 'In all there are forty-four phonemes in Mewati - fortyone segmental and three supra-segmental' (p. 1); the three suprasegmental phonemes are listed on p. 3 as Nasalisation, Length and Juncture (level/rising/falling terminal juncture, internal juncture). The 'Suprasegmental Features and Phonemes' section (pp. 74-77) treats pitch levels (normal, high, low), four terminal contours, intonation and juncture. Stress/accent is never mentioned in chapter I (TOC, a full-text search for stress/accent incl. letter-spaced variants, and reading of pp. 1-4 and 74-77).…

sources.citation: Srivastava, S. P. 2011. Mewati. In: Linguistic Survey of India: Rajasthan, Part I, pp. 247-324. Language Division, Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner, India.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number HC437.R3 C34 2014); the library holds the journal volume but the item itself was not found; ask your own library for a scan or interlibrary loan
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number HC437.R3 C34 2014
sources.note: 2.1.2 Suprasegmental Phonemes (p. 252): 'Length is not phonemic in Mewati. However the vowels /i I/, /u U/ and /A a/ exhibit contrast both in quality and quantity.. Mostly in mono-syllabic words (open or closed) the vowels tend to be long.' followed by nasalisation. 2.5 Syllable (pp. 271ff) gives syllable types and patterns. No statement about stress or accent anywhere in the Mewati chapter (full a full-text search for stress/accent pp. 247-324; the one 'stress' hit on p. 284 is a morphology sentence about feminine nouns).

sources.citation: Mathai, Eldose K. 2012. Sociolinguistic survey of selected Rajasthani speech varieties of Rajasthan, India, Volume 4: Mewati. SIL Electronic Survey Reports 2012-032.
sources.note: Only other recent Mewati-specific publication; sociolinguistic (RTT/questionnaires) so a stress statement is unlikely, but it may contain a wordlist appendix with phonetic transcription. PDF blocked (not reachable by automated download) by automated download.

sources.citation: Fatihi, A. R. 2005. The economy of articulation in Mewati phonology. Language in India 5(5), May 2005.
sources.note: Journal condensation of the thesis; clean text read in full. Covers Mewat, the Mewati sound system, cluster simplification, voiced/voiceless, aspirated/unaspirated, oral/nasal frequencies. No mention of stress, accent, tone or intonation.

sources.citation: Grierson, G. A. (ed.) 1908. Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. IX Part II: Specimens of the Rajasthani and Gujarati. Calcutta: Superintendent Government Printing. Mewati section pp. 45ff (grammar notes based on Macalister's Jaipur specimens).
sources.note: The Mewati sketch is 'very brief' and confined to points where the dialect differs from Jaipuri (declension, adjectives, verbs); no phonology and no accent statement. The only accent remark in the volume is the introductory transcription note that an acute accent marks an accented syllable where needed (not applied to Mewati).

sources.note: Only modern published sketch with a phonology chapter; the blurb explicitly comments on suprasegmentals ('not so prominent . in the other dialects of Rajasthani'), and Gusain's sibling LINCOM sketches of Rajasthani varieties carry one-line stress statements, so this is the likeliest place for an explicit Mewati stress rule.
